text: During backloading operation from a Drilling RIG to Platform Supply Vessel (PSV), a bundle of five 10''3/4 inch casing joints stacked on the deck of the PSV rolled over 2 deck crew (slingers). 29 x tubulars were already loaded (3 bundles x 5, 4 bundles x 3 and 2 x singles tubulars). 20 seconds after the last lift, the IPs were in front of the bundles rearranging the slings (in line of fire). IP1 had 1 leg trapped under the knee, IP2 (FAT) had 2 legs trapped under the knee. The rescue attempts freed IP1 (LTI) but resulted in the rest of the bundle collapsing on IP2. A tourniquet was applied on both legs and Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (CPR) was performed but was unsuccessful.

context.narrative: During backloading operation from a Drilling RIG to Platform Supply Vessel (PSV), a bundle of five 10''3/4 inch casing joints stacked on the deck of the PSV rolled over 2 deck crew (slingers). 29 x tubulars were already loaded (3 bundles x 5, 4 bundles x 3 and 2 x singles tubulars). 20 seconds after the last lift, the IPs were in front of the bundles rearranging the slings (in line of fire). IP1 had 1 leg trapped under the knee, IP2 (FAT) had 2 legs trapped under the knee. The rescue attempts freed IP1 (LTI) but resulted in the rest of the bundle collapsing on IP2. A tourniquet was applied on both legs and Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (CPR) was performed but was unsuccessful.
context.what_went_wrong:
1. Work preparation less than adequate: The risk analysis of the backloading operation did not identify the risk of tubular movement and personnel being crushed and therefore control measures were not implemented. There was also no lifting plan.
2. Equipment Guard/Tools not appropriate: No securing means have been used (wooden wedges, stanchions, ...) to mitigate the risk of tubular movement.
3. Supervision missing: There was no clear supervision of the loading operation. Nobody stopped the operation as it was being performed.
4. Rules not enforced: The recommendations for tubulars handling detailed in the Supply Vessel operation manual have not been implemented by the vessel technical operator.
5. Lack of regular visits/audits on safety aspects on PSV while in operation offshore.
6. No Training: No dedicated slinger/banksman training on PSV.
7. Rescue medical assistance: Lack of strong experience in emergency care on RIG. 8 Contractor selection - Absence of corrective action: No improvement plan developed after contract award of contractor with low HSE score.
context.corrective_actions:
• Laydown areas to be taken into consideration in risk analysis and lifting plans.
• Clarify responsibilities for marine operations within the 500m zone around installations.
• Ensure supervision on vessels.
• Emergency scenarios including Medevac from vessels to be included and tested.

text: On 2nd April 2025, an individual was found in between the sliding hydraulic watertight door (WTD) and the door frame. The individual was found unconscious and not breathing. The individual was brought to sick bay. The Incident Management Team was activated. Medics attended to the individual and assessed with no signs of life.

context.narrative: On 2nd April 2025, an individual was found in between the sliding hydraulic watertight door (WTD) and the door frame. The individual was found unconscious and not breathing. The individual was brought to sick bay. The Incident Management Team was activated. Medics attended to the individual and assessed with no signs of life.
context.what_went_wrong: The watertight door had been set to "Door Closed" mode, which activates an automatic closing mechanism after 10 seconds when the lever is released. The door movement closing time is no less than 20 seconds. The individual was in "Line of Fire" while passed through the WTD as it was automatically closing. Due to the significant force exerted by the watertight door, this resulted in the individual being trapped between the door and the frame.
context.corrective_actions:
1. The watertight door control mode was set to 'automatic close' based on site specific operating guidelines. The automatic watertight doors provide a Major Accident Event barrier for compartment flooding, but potentially pose a risk to personnel.
2. Familiarity with a known hazard, like a slow-moving watertight door, may create a false sense of safety and reduce perceived risk. Continuous reinforcement of hazard awareness is essential.
3. Encouraging teams to regularly discuss "what could go wrong", including unlikely or weak signals, helps maintain a sharp awareness of risks. By promoting curiosity, psychological safety, and learning from everyday work, organizations can strengthen their ability to guide safe behaviours and support effective human performance.

text: On 22 October 2025 at approximately 1615 hours, smoke alarm detectors were triggered in the engine room. Personnel on Board (POB) mustering and engine room reported one missing person. Emergency Response Team (ERT) deployed to the location and found one engine room operator unconscious, adjacent to steam plant. Additionally, there was sign of steam release found at site. Despite prompt medical attention by the onboard medical team, the individual was subsequently pronounced deceased. The affected equipment and piping were isolated.

context.narrative: On 22 October 2025 at approximately 1615 hours, smoke alarm detectors were triggered in the engine room. Personnel on Board (POB) mustering and engine room reported one missing person. Emergency Response Team (ERT) deployed to the location and found one engine room operator unconscious, adjacent to steam plant. Additionally, there was sign of steam release found at site. Despite prompt medical attention by the onboard medical team, the individual was subsequently pronounced deceased. The affected equipment and piping were isolated.
context.what_went_wrong:
This incident was due to the following factors:
a. Condensation-induced water hammer
b. The failure of the end plate weldment
c. The end plate was ejected and hit the DP on the right side of his head
context.corrective_actions: Gaps in system operation, monitoring, and competency management. This serves as an important reminder of the need for strong technical control and workforce awareness when operating steam systems. This incident highlights the importance of ensuring all crew, especially new and existing personnel, are properly trained and aware of steam system risks such as steam hammering, and are competent in following approved operating procedures. Critical equipment including control valves, steam traps, and piping must be maintained in proper working condition and operated in automatic mode where required to prevent condensate build-up and system damage. Adequate temperature and pressure monitoring must be in place and closely observed so that early intervention can be taken during abnormal conditions. Operating procedures must be regularly reviewed and updated to include steam hammering mitigation measures, and the Management of Change (MoC) process must be strengthened to ensure that any system modifications are properly assessed, documented, and reflected in as-built drawings.

text: During repair works on the Oil-Water Emulsion Heater at a Group Station, a fragment of a concrete block fell on a maintenance mechanic. The worker sustained severe physical injuries and passed away in the ambulance during transit to the hospital.

context.narrative: During repair works on the Oil-Water Emulsion Heater at a Group Station, a fragment of a concrete block fell on a maintenance mechanic. The worker sustained severe physical injuries and passed away in the ambulance during transit to the hospital.
context.what_went_wrong:
1. Unsafe Acts and Human Factors: Personnel applied an unauthorized "choke hitch" slinging method after the burner became stuck during the initial lifting attempt. The injured worker violated safety protocols by pulling himself up on the burner itself to secure the sling, using the equipment as a physical support. When technical difficulties arose (equipment jamming), the crew failed to stop work for a reassessment of risks, leading to the burner falling along with the worker.
2. Failures in Operational Control: The responsible line supervisor was absent from the high-risk work site, having left for another facility to perform a different task. Oversight regarding the adherence to safety requirements by responsible persons and the employer was deemed insufficient. Despite the existence of a permit-to-work, no actual risk assessment (dynamic risk assessment) was conducted directly at the work site prior to the task.
3. Organizational and Systemic Deficiencies: The technological regulations lacked step-by-step instructions for the dismantling and installation of the burner, leading to dangerous improvisation on-site. Insufficient training and qualification of workers for this specific type of hazardous work were identified. The internal control system failed to provide adequate supervision during the planning and resource allocation stages.
4. Technical Consequences: As a result of falling from height along with the burner, the worker sustained severe injuries. The worker passed away in the ambulance enroute to the hospital.
context.corrective_actions:
1. Operational Oversight and Supervision: High-risk activities must never be conducted without the continuous presence and active supervision of a designated line supervisor. Supervisors must prioritize safety oversight over secondary tasks; leaving a high-risk site unattended creates a critical vulnerability.
2. Risk Assessment and "Stop Work Authority": A formal risk assessment must be documented and registered before starting any maintenance or dismantling work. Personnel must be empowered and trained to exercise "Stop Work Authority" the moment a task deviates from the plan (e.g., equipment jamming) to perform a dynamic risk reassessment. No work should commence or continue if safety measures are not fully organized or if the situation changes unexpectedly.
3. Technical Documentation and Procedures: Technological regulations must include detailed, step-by-step instructions for specific hazardous tasks, such as burner dismantling, including approved slinging points and methods. All technical procedures should be reviewed to ensure they cover the full lifecycle of the task: setup, execution, and emergency contingencies
4. Competence and Training: Training programs must go beyond general safety and focus on specific, high-risk operational tasks to ensure workers are fully prepared for the technical challenges they may face. Regular safety briefings should reinforce the dangers of using equipment (like burners or piping) as physical supports or climbing aids.
5. Permit-to-Work (PTW) System: The PTW system must be strictly enforced and potentially digitized to ensure all safety barriers are verified and documented by responsible parties before work begins.

context.narrative: On July 10, 2025, at approximately 7:40 AM, while traveling along public road, a contractor minibus carrying four passengers and a driver was involved in a frontal collision with a third-party truck, which had a single occupant. A third vehicle, a car carrying three passengers, was also involved in the incident. As a result of the collision, one passenger from the minibus and the driver of the truck tragically lost their lives. The remaining minibus occupants sustained injuries of varying severity and were transported to hospital for treatment. The three passengers from the car were medically evaluated and later discharged. Emergency services and another contractor vehicle arrived within minutes, and emergency calls were made.
context.what_went_wrong: Preliminary indications suggest the car, traveling ahead of the minibus, may have crossed lanes and interacted with the truck, triggering a chain reaction that caused the truck to veer into the minibus's path. The crash occurred rapidly, leaving little time for evasive action. Two passengers who were not wearing seatbelts were ejected from the minibus upon impact. One passenger sustained fatal injuries, while the other was severely injured.
context.corrective_actions:
1. While Contractor HSSE Management processes are in place and HSSE risks are generally identified as high, inconsistent specification, documentation, and assurance of transport and driver safety requirements - particularly for personnel transportation - can lead to gaps in effective risk mitigation. Clear, consistent contract requirements, robust contractor and subcontractor transport safety capability assessments, aligned HSSE Plans, and disciplined assurance with tracked actions to closure are essential to ensure driver safety risks are adequately managed throughout the contract lifecycle.
2. Transport and driver safety risks were inconsistently identified, embedded, or assured within contractor scopes -particularly in multi-mode contracts - leading to gaps in critical controls such as seatbelt use, fatigue management, and safety technology deployment. Clear scope ownership and active contract holder engagement, as seen in road-transport-focused contracts, are essential to ensure consistent enforcement of legal requirements, driver readiness, and effective use of technology-enabled controls across all transport activities.
3. Emergency response arrangements were not sufficiently adapted for road transport and commuting scenarios, with plans, training, and exercises primarily focused on site-based emergencies. The absence of joint planning with contractors, limited consideration of regional infrastructure and communication constraints, unclear offsite roles and responsibilities, and poorly defined notification and activation protocols reduced preparedness and effectiveness for offsite incidents. Emergency response planning must explicitly address offsite transport risks and be jointly assured with contractors to ensure timely, coordinated, and effective response.

text: On 18 August 2025, a team was installing a 6-inch pipe over a 35-metre section between two lines. This pipe was also to be used during WO operations. During the operation, the team separated a 6-inch pipe from a 2-inch pipe, both of which had previously been tied together with cords. The supervisor was immediately informed, the control room was alerted, and emergency procedures were quickly implemented.

context.what_went_wrong:

Additionally, in cases where potentially falling aluminium composite panels have been reported, remedial actions to remove and reinstall such panels are not promptly executed, despite the high potential impact of a dropped panel.
2. Corrective action process not effectively implemented. - There has been recurring near misses involving dropped Aluminium Composite Panels in 2016, 2017, 2018, and 2024. However, corrective actions, such as implementing monthly and quarterly drop inspections, have not been sustained. Furthermore, planned preventive maintenance and other assurance activities that were instituted have not been consistently followed and remain areas requiring improvement. For instance, the annual integrity assessment for 2023 and 2024 were not conducted as planned.
context.corrective_actions:
1. Conduct an integrity inspection and assessment of the external of the entire building to identify any areas of loose cladding and fix them immediately to prevent any potential recurrence of the incident in the short term.
2. Re-institute the conduct of the annual inspection programme of the entire exterior of the building's facade to identify any areas of loose cladding and fix them immediately to prevent any potential dropped objects.

text: On 8 October 2025 on an offshore rig, a lifting operation was underway to land an 11.8 m, 2.67 ton bottom hole assembly (BHA) into a storage basket on the riser deck. During the final positioning, the BHA made a sudden uncontrolled movement. The forward end either contacted the basket edge, rotating the load toward the injured person, or the crane made an unintended movement. The injured person was positioned in a narrow space between riser guide posts with no escape route available. He had earlier climbed onto adjacent baskets and manually guided the load several times to open covers in the inner basket. The BHA struck him in the chest and compressed him against another basket. Emergency response was immediate, and medical evacuation was carried out via search and rescue (SAR) helicopter. The investigation identified multiple human, organisational, technical, and task-related contributors including lack of hands-free lifting, trainee crane operator without supervision, congested deck layout, communication challenges, inadequate planning, and procedural non-compliance.

context.narrative: On 8 October 2025 on an offshore rig, a lifting operation was underway to land an 11.8 m, 2.67 ton bottom hole assembly (BHA) into a storage basket on the riser deck. During the final positioning, the BHA made a sudden uncontrolled movement. The forward end either contacted the basket edge, rotating the load toward the injured person, or the crane made an unintended movement. The injured person was positioned in a narrow space between riser guide posts with no escape route available. He had earlier climbed onto adjacent baskets and manually guided the load several times to open covers in the inner basket. The BHA struck him in the chest and compressed him against another basket. Emergency response was immediate, and medical evacuation was carried out via search and rescue (SAR) helicopter. The investigation identified multiple human, organisational, technical, and task-related contributors including lack of hands-free lifting, trainee crane operator without supervision, congested deck layout, communication challenges, inadequate planning, and procedural non-compliance.
context.what_went_wrong: Hands-free lifting methods were not used despite being available, exposing personnel to the line of fire. The crane was operated by a trainee without required mentor supervision, contrary to procedure. The lift was treated as a routine task, and risk assessment did not account for congested deck layout, lack of escape routes, basket orientation requirements, or blind zones for the crane operator. The BHA was landed the wrong way due to missing communication, partly caused by language barriers. The deck was heavily congested, forcing the injured person into restricted and hazardous positions to open basket covers and guide the BHA manually. No exclusion zone was established. Several crew members were new in roles or on the rig, and norms for intervening or stopping unsafe work were inconsistent. Organisational follow-up on competence, planning quality, and supervision responsibilities was insufficient. These factors created multiple error traps and eliminated critical barriers.
context.corrective_actions: Lifting operations involving heavy BHA components require detailed planning that reflects actual deck conditions, special equipment requirements, and correct use of hands-free practices. Exclusion zones and escape routes must always be established and maintained. Trainee crane operators must only operate under direct mentor supervision in accordance with formal competence requirements. Communication expectations with third-party vendors must be clear, including language-barrier mitigation. Deck layout planning between logistics and lifting operations must ensure safe accessibility, visibility, and controlled load movement. Stop-work authority must be reinforced culturally to empower all personnel to intervene. Competence verification prior to mobilisation and clearer integration of procedures into workflow are essential to prevent recurrence.

text: An operator was removing a grating panel with manual handling hooks on the weather deck. During the operation, the grating unhooked from the manual handling tools and fell through the opening, hit a cable gate before landing on the underlying deck, approximately 10 meters below. The grating measures 1x1 meter and weighs 52,4 kg which gives a kinetic energy of 5149, 44 Joules. No one was injured, but under slightly changed circumstances people could have been in the line of fire as the deck was not cordoned off and there was a work team close to the area where it dropped.

context.narrative: An operator was removing a grating panel with manual handling hooks on the weather deck. The grating measures 1x1 meter and weighs 52,4 kg which gives a kinetic energy of 5149, 44 Joules. No one was injured, but under slightly changed circumstances people could have been in the line of fire as the deck was not cordoned off and there was a work team close to the area where it dropped.
context.what_went_wrong: The grating was not physically secured. During job preparation, the work crew had not reviewed all the required safety measures before starting the job, nor verified that they had been implemented, such as securing tools and equipment to prevent them from falling and barricading the area below the work site. No supervisor present to correct.
context.corrective_actions:
• When working at height, it is essential to ensure that tools and equipment are secured to prevent falling objects, in accordance with life-saving rules.
• When installing grating, it must always be secured with a fixed barrier, such as a shackle or wire/sling (the two-barrier principle), as shown in the image to the right.
• Grating like this should be secured to the structure above the work area. The securing equipment should be as short as practically possible.
• The area below must always be sufficiently cordoned off.

text: During platform crane lifting operations to land a container on the main deck North landing, the IP sustained a crush/impact injury to shoulder/ribs. The crane and container were made safe and the individual treated by platform advanced first aider followed by coastguard medevac for further assessment.

context.narrative: During platform crane lifting operations to land a container on the main deck North landing, the IP sustained a crush/impact injury to shoulder/ribs. The crane and container were made safe and the individual treated by platform advanced first aider followed by coastguard medevac for further assessment.
context.what_went_wrong:
• No verbal communication from banksman to crane operator of bridle being located in skip or not yet disconnected at time of verbal instruction "Up on your line".
• Banksman did not give clear communications to the crane operator and no use of confirmatory communications / protocols.
• No agreed set terminology or signals for free hook.
• No information passed to crane operator that the hook was in the skip and there were issues with disconnecting it.
• No crane motion instruction should have been issued by the banksman to the crane operator whilst the slinger was in the line of fire position.
• Poor communications led to assumption by crane operator that the hook was free.
• Banksman did not instruct Slinger to move out of Line of Fire prior to instructing Crane Op to go "Up on your line".
context.corrective_actions: There is no such thing as a routine activity - there are only repeat activities under different conditions that each needs to be understood and risk assessed. Maintain vigilance at all times. Safety Critical verbal communications need to be clear, concise and unambiguous to minimise the risk of incorrect interpretation. In safety critical tasks where there is no visual contact between work party members, confirmatory verbal communication should be used to verify understanding of commands (e.g. blind lifts, applying inhibits). Hazards may be constantly changing in nature throughout an activity. Wherever possible, removing the hazard or work parties' exposure to the hazard should be the priority in risk assessment- in this case "line of fire". text: A forklift driver's ankle was struck by a spreader bar during offloading from a truck at the logistics base. There were no lifting pockets welded onto the bar. In past lifting operations, the spreader bar had been placed on wooden blocks on the truck bed and lifted directly on the forks of a forklift. This time the wooden blocks were not in place. The truck driver and the forklift driver decided to lift the spreader bar off the truck by hooking hoisting slings attached to the spreader bar and to the forklift forks, crossing them to reduce the length of the slings. During hoisting, the spreader bar rotated and swung into the forklift cabin, hitting the driver's ankle. The forklift cabin door had been left open to improve communication between the drivers.

context.what_went_wrong:
1. Uncontrolled movement of the spreader bar due to hoisting the bar with slings hung from the forklift forks.
2. Forklift door left open for verbal communication.
3. Use of incorrect equipment to carry out the lift - it is forbidden to put slings directly onto the forks of a forklift, the spreader bar was not equipped with forklift pockets, a forklift hoisting adaptor was not available, a crane lift should have been utilised.
4. No lifting plan, job instructions or procedures in place, thus no management of change applied.
5. Inadequate induction and training for forklift drivers and visiting truck drivers.
6. Supervisor absent due to long-lasting illness, no official replacement.
7. High turnover of personnel at the logistics base.
context.corrective_actions:
1. Ensure all lifts performed with Forklift are covered by a procedure or lifting plan.
2. Specify the requirements for lifting operations in site training and induction programmes for the appropriate supply base personnel.
3. Check that the equipment needed to adapt forklifts for the expected loads is in place at site, and Operators are trained to safely use it.

text: On an offshore drilling rig, on 1 September 2025, personnel and marine crew were installing handrails on top of a unit on the main deck. Handrail sections (60-90 kg) were lifted by deck crane to the top of the unit, where an operator worked at height to receive and install them, using fall-arrest equipment. The operator initially attached his lanyard to the stairs, then to handrail, and later to another section to reach the final corner section. To fit the last section, he had to lift and adjust some of the handrail. The locking pins were weakly retained and the chain/carabiner secondary securing arrangement did not prevent them from sliding out. The section of the handrail tilted and fell, pulling the operator with it. He fell approximately 4.3 m to deck, landing partly on the fallen handrail. The incident resulted in an LTI and a dropped object with calculated energy of 2733 J, with assessed potential for a single fatality.

context.narrative: On an offshore drilling rig, on 1 September 2025, personnel and marine crew were installing handrails on top of a unit on the main deck. Handrail sections (60-90 kg) were lifted by deck crane to the top of the unit, where an operator worked at height to receive and install them, using fall-arrest equipment. The operator initially attached his lanyard to the stairs, then to handrail, and later to another section to reach the final corner section. To fit the last section, he had to lift and adjust some of the handrail. The locking pins were weakly retained and the chain/carabiner secondary securing arrangement did not prevent them from sliding out. The section of the handrail tilted and fell, pulling the operator with it. He fell approximately 4.3 m to deck, landing partly on the fallen handrail. The incident resulted in an LTI and a dropped object with calculated energy of 2733 J, with assessed potential for a single fatality.
context.what_went_wrong: The units were not designed to support safe work at height: the only structurally adequate anchoring points (lifting eyes) were located below top deck level and were occupied by lifting bridles during installation, leaving no suitable anchor points available. The operator therefore clipped his fall-arrest lanyard to a handrail section that was only temporarily secured by a pin, chain, and carabiner. The handrail securing design was inherently weak; on the short side of the container, the locking pin had only ~2 mm mechanical engagement and could easily slide out, and the chain/carabiner arrangement offered a false sense of security. The installation and commissioning procedure mentioned work at height and scaffolding, but did not clearly explain how the handrails should be installed or secured, nor the purpose or requirement for scaffold. No scaffold was erected, and the crew changed the intended installation sequence, requiring lifting and moving the section used as an anchor. Competence requirements for work at height (Norog 113) were not formalised in the competence matrix; several involved personnel lacked formal practical WAH training and were unaware of approved anchor point requirements. Project planning and follow-up from onshore were insufficient, and the contractor equipment checklist process was not effectively applied.
context.corrective_actions: Work at height must never rely on temporary structures (such as partially installed handrails) as anchoring points. Units that require routine or installation work at height must be designed with suitable, certified anchor points, or work must be carried out from properly designed scaffolding or other engineered access solutions. Competence requirements for working at height (incl. practical training and anchor-point assessment) must be explicitly built into contractor competence matrices and verified before mobilisation. Installation and commissioning procedures for vendor packages must clearly describe safe installation methods, including detailed handrail installation sequences, locking mechanisms, and when scaffolding is mandatory. Work permits that bundle many high-risk activities can obscure critical controls; large scopes should be broken into smaller work procedures where necessary to ensure hazards and controls are fully understood. A robust equipment and project-follow-up process is needed, including use of the correct contractor equipment checklist and clear assignment of onshore and offshore responsibility for installation planning and oversight.

text: Collision between northern crane and derrick resulting in falling objects. Three objects fell after the north crane collided with the derrick. The crane operator had been planning to perform lubrication of the slewing ring with the logistics discipline responsible for some time, but this was changed to the crane operator bringing along a deck operator who was being trained as a crane-operator. A helicopter was on its way to the platform, and they had about 25 minutes to finish before the helicopter arrived. It was decided that the crane operator was to perform the lubrication in the crane pedestal while the deck operator operated the crane. The crane was lifted and swung out over the sea. The crane operator reminded to "elevate the crane-boom" to avoid the derrick and then went down into the pedestal. The deck operator elevated the boom and swung the crane towards the platform. After a brief stop to change the lubrication cartridge, the crane was topped up a little more before it swung further towards the derrick. The deck operator believed the boom was topped up enough. The walkway and the spotlight mounted on the right side of the boom were driven into the upper corner of the wind wall high up in the derrick. At the same time, the crane was lifted somewhat and detached from the tower. The crane shook, and the deck operator observed an object fall into an area where personnel were normally present. After receiving information about what had happened over the radio, the crane operator came to the cabin, took over, and lowered the crane into the cradle. The logistics discipline responsible heard what was being said on the radio, responded, and found the spotlight in a pallet with wooden lids in the moonpool area. A section of weather protection from the derrick was found a few minutes later, and a bracket for securing electrical cables was found three days later on a walkway one level above the moonpool area.

text: Two personnel experienced symptoms of severe oxygen deficiency during inspection work, but managed to self-evacuate safely. Subsequent measurements confirmed low oxygen levels inside the enclosure, linked to nitrogen ingress from the turbine seal system combined with a lack of ventilation.

context.narrative: Two personnel experienced symptoms of severe oxygen deficiency during inspection work, but managed to self-evacuate safely. Subsequent measurements confirmed low oxygen levels inside the enclosure, linked to nitrogen ingress from the turbine seal system combined with a lack of ventilation.
context.what_went_wrong: The incident was triggered by nitrogen leakage from the seal system, which under normal ventilated conditions is harmless. However, following a planned emergency shutdown (ESD) and blackstart prior to shutdown period, key barriers were unavailable: ventilation remained off, and the fire dampers which require manual reopening, stayed closed. Without airflow, oxygen was gradually displaced overnight creating a hazardous atmosphere that posed a serious risk of unconsciousness and fatality.
context.corrective_actions: Assess feasibility of installing fixed oxygen monitoring in the turbine enclosure and similar areas. If not feasible, require mandatory portable gas testing before entry into locations with potential oxygen depletion risk. Review and update the blackstart procedure to ensure turbine hood ventilation and dampers are restored before the area is reclassified as safe for entry. Revise PTW requirements for entries into the turbine enclosure during or after special operational states (e.g., blackstart, shutdown, or loss of HVAC). The PTW must account for potential atmospheric changes, with mandatory portable gas measurements under such conditions.

text: During preparations for installing a 20'' sealing ring on the platform on 2 July 2025, a technician tested the ring for fit before the lift operation. The 7.1 kg ring slipped from the technician's hands and fell 6.35 meters to the deck below, landing approximately two meters from a mechanic who was grinding at deck level. The ring then bounced and struck the mechanic on the arm. The mechanic received a first-aid level impact with no observable injury. The event had a severe potential for fatality due to the weight and fall height. The ring had been brought into the elevated work area earlier than planned, the area was insufficiently barricaded, and the test occurred without notification to the crew below. Multiple procedural, communication and barrier-management weaknesses contributed.

context.narrative: During preparations for installing a 20'' sealing ring on the platform on 2 July 2025, a technician tested the ring for fit before the lift operation. The 7.1 kg ring slipped from the technician's hands and fell 6.35 meters to the deck below, landing approximately two meters from a mechanic who was grinding at deck level. The ring then bounced and struck the mechanic on the arm. The mechanic received a first-aid level impact with no observable injury. The event had a severe potential for fatality due to the weight and fall height. The ring had been brought into the elevated work area earlier than planned, the area was insufficiently barricaded, and the test occurred without notification to the crew below. Multiple procedural, communication and barrier-management weaknesses contributed.
context.what_went_wrong: The sealing ring was tested earlier than planned, without expanding the barricaded area and without informing the crew below. The ring slipped due to inadequate handling conditions (gloves, oily surface). The work area had been split into two phases, but equipment was still placed in the elevated area during phase one, creating exposure before barriers were in place. Barricading was too small, based on a common but unsafe practice of using minimal exclusion zones for "non-loose object" work at height. Communication between team members and between teams and was incomplete. The area technician approved only the intent of barricading but did not verify it physically. The team lead was cognitively overloaded and new in the role, reducing situational awareness. Stop-work authority was not used despite unease among personnel below. The net result was coexistence of workers above and below with no effective barrier against dropped objects.
context.corrective_actions: All work at height must assume potential for falling objects and require full barricading unless a technical barrier (e.g., safety net) is installed. Equipment must not be brought into elevated areas before controls are in place. Area technicians must physically verify barricades before work starts. Practices that rely on personnel remembering not to bring loose items into height work are insufficient; technical and organizational barriers must supplement human behaviour. SIMOPS coordination must be strengthened, including explicit identification of all nearby work teams and discussion in morning meetings. Communication internally within teams must be improved to ensure shared situational awareness. Stop-work authority must be normalised, supported, and used proactively. Project-wide learning should be shared across platforms to eliminate similar practices elsewhere.

text: During the night shift, the crew attempted to release an anchor latch tool from a permanent packer using a straight pull of 60 klbs (including 55 klbs string weight) without success. Following contractors' procedures, the string was tensioned with 5 klbs over string weight and rotated manually, but no movement was observed. Based on contractors' instructions, power tongs were partially used due to the absence of a power swivel on site. During the sixth right-hand turn with a 5 klbs overpull, the 2-7/8" tubing coupling connected to the safety valve backed off and fell approximately 21 ft onto the rig floor, then a further 14 ft to the ground. At the same time, the tubing string settled approximately 6 ft into the packer. The combined weight of the coupling and safety valve was 36.5 kg.

context.narrative: During the night shift, the crew attempted to release an anchor latch tool from a permanent packer using a straight pull of 60 klbs (including 55 klbs string weight) without success. Following contractors' procedures, the string was tensioned with 5 klbs over string weight and rotated manually, but no movement was observed. Based on contractors' instructions, power tongs were partially used due to the absence of a power swivel on site. During the sixth right-hand turn with a 5 klbs overpull, the 2-7/8" tubing coupling connected to the safety valve backed off and fell approximately 21 ft onto the rig floor, then a further 14 ft to the ground. At the same time, the tubing string settled approximately 6 ft into the packer. The combined weight of the coupling and safety valve was 36.5 kg.
context.what_went_wrong:
1. Uncontrolled rotation using a power tong led to the tubing connection backing off.
2. Thread make-up integrity was not sufficient for rotation under tension.
3. Lack of appropriate equipment (power swivel) resulted in the use of a higher-risk alternative.
4. Dropped-object controls were inadequate, allowing heavy equipment to fall from height.
context.corrective_actions:
1. Management of Change (MoC) must be applied before deviation. Any deviation from approved procedures, tooling, or operating limits shall be formally reviewed, risk-assessed, and approved through the MBPS MoC process prior to execution.
2. Operations must stop when normal operating parameters are exceeded. When loads, methods, or equipment differ from the original plan, supervisors must stop work and reassess using approved Operator procedures and MoC requirements.
3. Contractually required equipment must be available and used as intended. Operations shall not proceed unless all contract-specified rig equipment is present, functional, and fit for purpose. Temporary or partial substitutions are not acceptable.
4. Stop Work Authority (SWA) must be actively exercised and enforced. All personnel are required to stop work when unsafe conditions exist, including dropped-object exposure, lack of secondary retention, or use of non-approved tools or methods.
5. Secondary retention is mandatory for elevated components. All elevated or moving tools and components shall be secured with secondary retention wherever practicable to prevent dropped-object incidents.
6. Roles and scopes of work must be clearly understood and respected. Operators and service providers shall operate strictly within their defined scopes of work, with no overreach beyond assigned responsibilities.

After disconnecting the hoses, the contractor field service representative was on the back side of the gas turbine while the mechanical technicians were on the front side. While lying beneath the gas turbine to check the water wash drain tube under the gas turbine, pressure was released, causing the loose hoses to swing.
context.what_went_wrong: One of the loose hoses struck the helmet of the mechanical field service representative, resulting in physical damage to the helmet.
context.corrective_actions:
• Trapped pressure must always be safely discharged before disconnecting components, even when the system appears isolated - especially in high-pressure gas systems.
• Contractor activities must be fully integrated into company isolation procedures, including proper documentation in Process Isolation Certificates, to avoid oversight of critical steps.
• Safe Work Method Statements (SWMS) must include detailed, step-by-step instructions, particularly for non-routine tasks, to ensure consistent understanding and execution.
• Non-routine activities require Task Risk Assessments (TRA) regardless of pressure levels or perceived risk, as they often involve unexpected hazards.
• System manipulations (e.g., Programmable Logic Controller forcing) must not occur without coordination and approval from the Area Authority, and only after confirming all personnel are in safe positions.

context.corrective_actions:

• Always use additional support systems like rubber mats and/or dunnage to increase the clamp down effect (friction between the load and the trailer surface) to prevent the load from shifting.
• Always ensure loading crews and driver clearly understand the importance of the pre-trip Inspection - lashing belts and tools must be thoroughly inspected for wear, damage, and suitability before departure. Early detection of weakened or compromised equipment can prevent incidents.
• Always ensure corrective actions are implemented at the earliest opportunity to prevent recurrence of similar incidents/accidents - there was a similar incident three months earlier.

context.what_went_wrong:

context.corrective_actions:
• Any equipment damage, substitution, or deviation from approved design shall trigger immediate STOP WORK and be subject to a formal Management of Change process prior to resuming operations.
• Secondary retention devices are safety-critical controls and shall not be removed, bypassed, or omitted without formal engineering justification and authorization.
• Critical procedural requirements must be complied with at all times, without exception, including during routine, non-routine, and close-out activities.
• Always follow red zone management, no simultaneous activities during rig-down.

text: The rig crew were in the process of nipple down the bell nipple mandrel. While positioning the multi purpose crane for installing the bell nipple lifting slings the man basket (354kg), which was holding 2 persons, dislodged from the main structure of the crane and fell approx.16.5m to the top deck of the platform. Neither of the 2 persons fell as they were suspended by their harness and inertia reels. Both personnel were recovered in 2 minutes. One of the 2 personnel received first aid treatment for slight swelling.

context.narrative: The rig crew were in the process of nipple down the bell nipple mandrel. While positioning the multi purpose crane for installing the bell nipple lifting slings the man basket (354kg), which was holding 2 persons, dislodged from the main structure of the crane and fell approx.16.5m to the top deck of the platform. Neither of the 2 persons fell as they were suspended by their harness and inertia reels. Both personnel were recovered in 2 minutes. One of the 2 personnel received first aid treatment for slight swelling.
context.what_went_wrong:
1. Rotation of man basket around crane winch drum collar created momentum:
a) System has always been "sticky" with the man basket not self-levelling.
b) Rig crew have developed processes to correct (jumping and operate the winch slightly) that are not included in the procedures.
2. Crane wire fitted with shackle caught on man basket structure resulted in lift forces.
3. Combination of forces resulted in man basket lifting and twisting away from the sheave.
4. Multipurpose Crane not being operated as per OEM requirements when DMB installed:
a) Man-basket should not move independently of the crane sheave.
b) Moving the controls to the man basket is a requirement within the manual. This releases the drive motor from the sheave and allows the sheave to rotate freely.
5. Man-basket safety device deployed but not effective:
a) Deemed ineffective following a past incident at another location.
b) OEM's recommendations regarding the new design and the additional inspections were not considered.
context.corrective_actions:
1. Reinforce the importance of using independent fall arrest equipment when working at height
2. Reinforce the requirement carefully considering attachment points for fall arrest equipment.
3. Ensure that fall arrest equipment is inspected and certified as per Company Procedure.
4. Reinforce the importance of maintaining, storing and inspecting all safety critical equipment to ensure it is in excellent working order when being used.

context.corrective_actions:

• Review the competency levels of personnel involved in lifting operations and provide retraining where gaps are identified.
• Issue a formal communication requiring permit-to-work compliance and task-specific risk assessments for all non-routine activities within designated safety zones.
• Amend the company standard to formally include the prohibition of tag lines and the requirement to maintain a clear deck policy during boat lifting operations.

text: On May 20, 2025, a worker was engaged in repositioning a spec blind from the closed to the open position on the flare line, in preparation to de-isolate the unit for commissioning activities. During this activity, the worker was exposed to a gas/energy release from the down steam side of the isolated gate valve at the open flange pair. Worker required rescue from heights and was provided onsite first aid; worker was transported to a local hospital for further medical assessment where it was determined worker sustained bruised ribs and a concussion. Worker was released from hospital the same day.

context.narrative: On May 20, 2025, a worker was engaged in repositioning a spec blind from the closed to the open position on the flare line, in preparation to de-isolate the unit for commissioning activities. During this activity, the worker was exposed to a gas/energy release from the down steam side of the isolated gate valve at the open flange pair. Worker required rescue from heights and was provided onsite first aid; worker was transported to a local hospital for further medical assessment where it was determined worker sustained bruised ribs and a concussion. Worker was released from hospital the same day.
context.what_went_wrong: The 10" gate valve used as a single isolation was not fully closed because the chain operator seized due to physical interference, giving a false indication that the valve was seated. Pressure verification showed 0 kPag, but this was ambiguous because the flare system was under slight vacuum, meaning zero pressure did not confirm positive isolation. Oxygen entered the flare piping system through the partially open valve while the flare remained lit, creating conditions for ignition. When work was performed on the spectacle blind, this led to a deflagration and an uncontrolled release of energy that injured the worker.
context.corrective_actions:
1. Zero pressure does not equal positive isolation - Pressure indication alone is an insufficient barrier for verifying isolation in flare systems, especially where vacuum conditions can exist.
2. Single isolation is not a robust barrier for breaking containment - Single isolation provides little tolerance for hidden failures and should not be relied upon where severe energy release is credible.
3. Equipment condition and work environment directly shape human decision-making - People act on the cues the system gives them; degraded equipment and obstructed layouts can actively mislead competent workers.
4. Permits and risk classification must reflect real hazard potential - Administrative controls lose credibility when they do not reflect the true severity of the hazard.

The job was stopped, emergency medical response was initiated, and the well/site was shut down to support response and control the release.
context.what_went_wrong: Residual energy remained in the system at the time of disconnection/valve manipulation, resulting in a hot-fluid spray. context.corrective_actions: Update procedures and minimum PPE requirements for hot-fluid tasks (including defined thresholds) and incorporate explicit "verify zero energy" expectations. Where verification is not practicable, implement engineering/administrative improvements (e.g., bleed/verification points or safer valve/coupler configurations) so that residual energy can be confirmed and controlled before disconnecting equipment.

text: A worker fell approximately 16 feet from an aerial work platform onto a Christmas tree cart. The incident occurred while the worker was using a rope tied to the basket to pull an umbilical and create slack for a storm loop. context.narrative: A worker fell approximately 16 feet from an aerial work platform onto a Christmas tree cart. The incident occurred while the worker was using a rope tied to the basket to pull an umbilical and create slack for a storm loop. The rope failed under tension, releasing stored energy that transferred to the basket. This sudden release caused the basket to jolt, ejecting the worker.
context.what_went_wrong: The task was executed outside equipment design intent, with a man-riding work basket simultaneously used to pull a load, creating uncontrolled stored energy and disabling effective engineered safeguards. The activity was not recognised or managed as a lifting operation, resulting in inadequate planning, inappropriate equipment selection, and exposure of a person to the line of fire when the rope failed. These failures were reinforced by unclear procedures, fragmented task briefings, and ineffective supervision, allowing unsafe deviations to become normalised.
context.corrective_actions:
1. Inspection and maintenance for man-riding and lifting equipment must meet or exceed manufacturer requirements, particularly under heavy or harsh operating conditions. Inspection scope, frequency, and competency should scale with equipment usage and environmental exposure - not minimum internal checklists.
2. Checklist effectiveness depends as much on quality, compliance, and competency as the checklist itself. Poor design, superficial completion, or unclear roles can create false assurance and allow serious hazards to persist.
3. Safe operation of critical equipment requires clear, shared accountability across suppliers, contractors, and asset owners. Pre-mobilization checks, acceptance inspections, condition monitoring, and post-event inspections must be treated as mandatory control points throughout the equipment lifecycle - not administrative steps.

context.what_went_wrong:

• Insufficient communication with vessel captain.
• While all safety measures on the platform and by the diving team were followed, the control barrier against external vessel movements failed.

• The incident primarily resulted from lack of effective marine coordination and vessel traffic control, leading to a near-miss with potentially severe consequences for diving operations.
context.corrective_actions:
• Ensure all vessels operating near offshore platforms are aware of ongoing diving operations.
• Strengthen coordination with support vessels and vessel traffic control to enforce exclusion zones proactively.
• Establish mandatory pre-approach notifications for all vessels near the platform.
• Ensure immediate and continuous communication channels between the platform, diving team, and vessel captains.

text: During the inspection of the 8-inch subsea oil and gas pipeline located between offshore platforms, diving operations were in progress and a scheduled descent from the diving vessel had commenced. The diver was immediately recovered from the water, and the vessel proceeded toward the platform, where it was safely moored at the docking bridge. Following the safe disembarkation of personnel, the damaged vessel was towed to the onshore port by an assisting tugboat.

context.narrative: During the inspection of the 8-inch subsea oil and gas pipeline located between offshore platforms, diving operations were in progress and a scheduled descent from the diving vessel had commenced. Approximately 15 minutes after the diver entered the water, the vessel's mechanic reported hull damage resulting in water ingress into the engine room. The diver was immediately recovered from the water, and the vessel proceeded toward the platform, where it was safely moored at the docking bridge. Following the safe disembarkation of personnel, the damaged vessel was towed to the onshore port by an assisting tugboat.
context.what_went_wrong:
• Failure of Vessel Structural Integrity
• Inadequate Pre-Operation Marine Assurance and possible gaps in seaworthiness verification of the vessel
• Inadequate preventive maintenance controls
• Inadequate hull condition monitoring
• Inadequate pre-mobilization inspection and certification checks.
context.corrective_actions:
• Pre-operation marine inspections must be robust
• Pre-mobilization and daily checks should include:
• Hull condition verification
• Corrosion and structural damage inspection
• Confirmation of valid marine certification
• Review of maintenance status
• Inspection processes must be documented and traceable.

context.what_went_wrong:
• The torch was not in optimal condition (the built-in/manual spark igniter did not work properly).
• Low perception of risk when lighting a torch in a closed environment.
• Incorrect Work Permit (PTW), classified the activity as "cold work" when in fact it involved "high-energy hot work" with the generation of ignition sources.
context.corrective_actions:
• Emphasize the responsibilities of workers with roles in the PTW system in the event of serious or fatal workplace accidents involving their own workers or contractors.
• Conduct an awareness campaign (including contractors) on inspection, reporting, and replacement of tools and equipment in poor condition (homemade or artisanal tools) before the end of the year.

text:
During production tubing running operations on the drilling rig, four metallic components fell from height while using the catline system.
• Objects dropped from approximately 40 m height
• 2 × 1.8 kg (≈ 706 J each)
• 2 × 10.4 kg (≈ 4,076 J each) The falling energy was sufficient to cause a fatality. No injuries occurred, but this qualifies as a High Potential Event (HIPO) due to the severe dropped-object energy.

context.narrative:
During production tubing running operations on the drilling rig, four metallic components fell from height while using the catline system.
• Objects dropped from approximately 40 m height
• 2 × 1.8 kg (≈ 706 J each)
• 2 × 10.4 kg (≈ 4,076 J each) The falling energy was sufficient to cause a fatality. No injuries occurred, but this qualifies as a High Potential Event (HIPO) due to the severe dropped-object energy.
context.what_went_wrong:
• Catline anchoring point and installation were modified from the original design without engineering review.
• Assembly was improperly installed and inadequately supported (misaligned rods/spacers, gaps in fittings).
• Refurbished and reused components were not integrity tested; the installed system was not certified to required load capacity.
• No Management of Change (MOC), risk assessment, or formal operator approval for the modification.
• PTW/JSA did not address the installation change or dropped-object risk.
• Poor communication and oversight between operator and contractor; no operator supervision of the work.
context.corrective_actions:
• Treat any change to lifting/hoisting equipment or anchoring as a design change requiring MOC, risk assessment, and operator approval.
• Certification must cover the complete installed system, not only individual components, and must meet operational load requirements.
• Verify integrity of reused or refurbished parts before use.
• Ensure PTW/JSA reflects actual installation and hazards.
• Clearly define contractor-operator responsibilities and provide supervision for safety-critical work.
• Conduct formal dropped-object inspections after maintenance or modification to derrick equipment.

text: On 17 November at approximately 09:40, the smoke detector in the laundry room activated after several cleaning cloths spontaneously combusted shortly after being removed from a dryer and placed on the floor. The fire brigade responded immediately and extinguished the fire using CO2 and dry powder extinguishers. No injuries or asset damage occurred, but the event had potential for a serious fire and smoke exposure.

context.narrative: On 17 November at approximately 09:40, the smoke detector in the laundry room activated after several cleaning cloths spontaneously combusted shortly after being removed from a dryer and placed on the floor. The fire brigade responded immediately and extinguished the fire using CO2 and dry powder extinguishers. No injuries or asset damage occurred, but the event had potential for a serious fire and smoke exposure.
context.what_went_wrong:
• Cleaning cloths were likely contaminated with a chemical/oily substance capable of self-heating after drying.
• The chemical hazard was not identified prior to washing and drying.
• Hot cloths were stacked/placed on the floor immediately after drying, allowing heat build-up and ignition.
• No procedure or segregation process existed for handling contaminated rags.
• Personnel did not recognise the chemical odour as a hazard indicator.
context.corrective_actions:
• Treat cleaning rags as potentially oil/chemical contaminated materials.
• Implement segregation and identification of contaminated cloths before laundering.
• Allow hot cloths to cool in a ventilated metal container or spread individually -do not pile them.
• Provide training on spontaneous combustion risks (especially oils, solvents, and hydrocarbons).
• Establish procedures for laundering and disposal of contaminated rags.
• Provide dedicated fire-safe storage bins for used cleaning cloths.

causal_factors.factor: Improper decision making or lack of judgment
Inadequate hazard identification or risk assessment

text: On 27 December at approximately 07:30, cleaning cloths contaminated with cooking oil were washed and dried in the laundry. After drying, the cloths were placed on the floor inside an open bag next to other cloths. Later, all laundry ventilation, exhaust, and air-conditioning systems were switched off while the room was unattended. At approximately 13:15, the cloths began releasing smoke and an incipient fire developed. The steward used a dry chemical extinguisher and the fire brigade extinguished the fire. No injuries or damage occurred, but the event had serious fire potential.

context.narrative: On 27 December at approximately 07:30, cleaning cloths contaminated with cooking oil were washed and dried in the laundry. After drying, the cloths were placed on the floor inside an open bag next to other cloths. Later, all laundry ventilation, exhaust, and air-conditioning systems were switched off while the room was unattended. At approximately 13:15, the cloths began releasing smoke and an incipient fire developed. The steward used a dry chemical extinguisher and the fire brigade extinguished the fire. No injuries or damage occurred, but the event had serious fire potential.
context.what_went_wrong:
• Oil-contaminated cloths were washed and dried without special handling precautions.
• Hot cloths were stored in a pile/bag, allowing heat accumulation and self-heating.
• Laundry ventilation and cooling were shut down while the cloths were unattended.
• No procedure existed for segregation, cooling, or disposal of oily rags.
• Hazard of spontaneous combustion from oil-soaked rags was not recognised.
context.corrective_actions:
• Segregate oil/grease contaminated cloths before laundering.
• Do not place recently dried cloths in piles, bags, or enclosed areas - allow them to cool individually in a ventilated metal container or spread out.
• Maintain ventilation/exhaust until materials have cooled.
• Implement procedures for handling and disposal of contaminated rags.
• Train personnel on spontaneous combustion risks (oils, hydrocarbons, solvents).
• Provide fire-resistant rag bins and designated storage areas.

text: Three employees for J&R Transport were onsite when a flash fire occurred at an oil/gas wellsite. J&R Transport was hired to clean heater treater equipment at the wellsite. The heater treater had been removed from the oil/gas well system and was placed adjacent to the well head. A roustabout crew from another employer was onsite and removed the bolts and fire tube from the heater treater. When the tire tube was removed, a black liquid came out of the heater treater and spilled onto the ground and surrounding area. J&R Transport performed vacuum truck operations to remove the liquid from the ground. When that was complete, two J&R Transport employees began power washing the inside of the heater treater. One employee operated the power washer wand while the other employee operated the vacuum truck's suction hose. During this operation, a flash fire occurred inside the heater treater vessel resulting in fire shooting from the open end of the vessel where the two employees were working. One employee was thrown backward and suffered fractures to his collar bone, ribs, and shoulder and burns to face and arms. The other employee suffered second degree burns to his hands and first degree burns to his face. One employee was hospitalized.

meta.event_type: Vehicle or machinery fire
